notes.title: Lead with evidence, not optimism
source: A useful status update separates evidence from interpretation. Start with an observable result: the checkout test passed 48 of 50 cases. Then name the remaining risk and the next check.
Avoid phrases such as “probably fixed” unless you also state the evidence and uncertainty. Your listener should know what happened, what remains uncertain, and what you will verify next.

questions.prompt: Give a three-part status update for a feature whose main test passes but two edge cases still fail.
questions.coachHint: Aim for an observed result, a remaining risk, and a next check.
questions.referenceAnswer: The main test passed, but two edge cases still fail, so the remaining risk is incomplete boundary handling. I will fix those cases and retest the full suite next.

questions.prompt: Why is “probably fixed” weaker than evidence-first language?
questions.coachHint: Explain what the listener cannot verify from that phrase.
questions.referenceAnswer: “Probably fixed” reports a belief, not observable evidence. It also hides the remaining uncertainty and gives no verification step, so the listener cannot judge the current risk.

notes.title: Explain the constraint before the choice
source: A technical decision becomes easier to evaluate when you explain four things in order: the constraint, the chosen option, the tradeoff, and the condition that would make you revisit it.
This structure shows judgment without pretending the choice is permanent. It also helps teammates challenge the right assumption instead of debating personal preference.

questions.prompt: Explain why your team chose a simple local cache instead of a distributed cache for a small prototype.
questions.coachHint: Name the present constraint, choice, tradeoff, and revisit condition.
questions.referenceAnswer: Because the prototype has one process and needs fast iteration, we chose a local cache. We accept that it will not share state across instances. We will revisit a distributed cache when we add a second instance or measure unacceptable inconsistency.

notes.title: Say what would change your mind
source: Calibrated uncertainty is more useful than vague caution. Give a confidence level, name the evidence behind it, and state what new information would change your view.

For example: “I have medium confidence because the integration test passes in staging, but I would lower it if production traffic reveals a different request pattern.” This makes uncertainty actionable.

questions.prompt: Report medium confidence that a release is safe after it passed in staging.
questions.coachHint: Include confidence, evidence, and a condition that would change your view.
questions.referenceAnswer: I have medium confidence that the release is safe because the integration test passed in staging. I would lower that confidence if production traffic shows a different request pattern or new errors.

criteria.label: Says what would change the view
